claims.text: The stability of equiatomic HEA nanoparticles across 473–1923 K is governed by the balance between configurational entropy and constituent-metal surface-energy differences.
Small differences in intrinsic surface energy suppress elemental surface segregation.
Suppression of surface segregation maintains a single-phase solid solution.
An element with substantially lower surface energy than the other constituents will segregate at elevated temperature.
Surface segregation of the low-surface-energy element leads to phase separation or oxidation.
Differential surface energies drive atomic diffusion at high temperature.
Similar constituent surface energies in the equiatomic baseline minimize elemental segregation.
Increasing the proportion of a low-surface-energy element enhances its surface segregation.
Enhanced segregation of the low-surface-energy element creates a distinct surface layer.
The segregated surface layer may passivate the nanoparticles.
The segregated surface layer may destabilize the nanoparticles through phase separation or oxidation.
Under the specified high-temperature conditions, the equiatomic control will largely retain its single-phase solid-solution structure.
Under the specified high-temperature conditions, the equiatomic control will show minimal measurable surface segregation.
Relative to the control, nanoparticles enriched in the low-surface-energy element will show measurable surface segregation.
Relative to the control, nanoparticles enriched in the low-surface-energy element will show earlier signs of phase decomposition or oxidation.
The surface-energy threshold for significant segregation may depend on the selected elements and operating atmosphere.
